About ESM

The first of its kind in Sri Lanka

Equi Space Med (ESM) began with a simple conviction: the science that keeps astronauts alive in orbit — how bodies adapt to microgravity, radiation, and isolation — holds answers for people on Earth too, especially those furthest from good healthcare.

We are the first space medicine initiative in Sri Lanka, built by and for university students who want to do real, collaborative research rather than wait for the field to arrive here on its own.

ESM started with 20 incredible students and is growing steadily, welcoming new members from medical and biomedical engineering faculties across the country's universities.

Founder

Abanthika Yogarasa

ESM was founded and is led by Abanthika Yogarasa, with the goal of giving Sri Lankan students a real seat in the emerging field of space medicine — and a way to turn that research into equal, translational benefit for everyone.

Translational health, drawn from space, delivered equally — until no one is left behind.

Everything ESM builds — every research group, every article, every experiment — is aimed at producing quality science that moves from orbit to everyday care, shared without gatekeeping.

What we do

Research, built together

Collaborative groups

Members form research groups across medicine and biomedical engineering, pairing clinical questions with engineering solutions.

Short & long-term projects

From quick investigations to sustained multi-month research, members choose the pace and depth that fits their work.

Published articles

ESM publishes original articles and findings on a steady rhythm — once every two months — keeping the work visible and accountable.

Current project

Building Sri Lanka's own 3D clinostat

In progress

A cost-effective, locally built 3D clinostat

A clinostat simulates microgravity conditions on the ground by continuously reorienting a sample, letting researchers study how biological material responds to conditions like those in orbit — without leaving Sri Lanka.

Our members are designing and building one from the ground up, engineered to be affordable without cutting corners on efficiency or reliability — laying the groundwork for space biology research to happen locally, for the first time.
